en: The white king keeps chasing: it attacks c8 and dreams of escorting the pawn from b7.
The white king gives up the eviction and drops back, hoping to push the pawn under its own protection.
Second only-move, second check. Note the route: a7-c8-d6 — every square of the circuit keeps an eye on a8 or on the white king's escort squares.

Fleeing to e7 looks reasonable — the knight "stays in touch" with c8 and c6. The tablebase is final: the position flips from drawn to LOST. From e7 the knight needs TWO hops to regain control of the promotion path… and White only needs two moves.

And the loop closes: the identical position of two moves ago. The white king can run the circuit as often as it likes — c8, d6 and b5 take turns forever. Drawn by repetition, one knight against a whole king.
The one quiet move of the dance — and still the only one that holds: from d6 the knight watches both b7 AND c8, the two squares the white king needs to escort its pawn.
The king steps one square away? The knight returns to its post at once. The blockade resumes as if nothing had happened.
Better still: with the king gone, the knight can even leave the blockade to ATTACK. From c6 it targets a7 — if the pawn ventures there, it will not leave.
The long-prepared push…
…loses the pawn on the spot. Knight versus bare king: the cleanest draw in the book. Remember the knight's two registers: blockader when the king presses, hunter the moment it lets go.
The pawn crosses the 6th-rank frontier — precisely the line beyond which a lone knight can no longer catch a rook's pawn.
The knight rushes back and even attacks the pawn — but a7 is defended by the king, and c6 does NOT control a8.
One tempo too late. The whole ending lives in this contrast: c8-d6-b5 hold the draw to the exact move, e7 loses by the exact move.

A knight can blockade a single pawn forever — but it exists in only one place at a time. Two passed pawns at opposite ends of the board ask it a question it has no answer to, provided they're far enough advanced.
The 6th rank on both sides: too late

Only one of the two pawns advances — but the knight can only face ONE threat at a time, and the other pawn, still on h6, waits its turn with nothing in its way. One rank earlier (5th instead of 6th), the SAME position holds: the centrally-posted knight then has time to gallop from wing to wing. The rank alone decides.
The knight tries to intercept along the way — but he can only be in one place, and there's always one pawn too many.
Too late to stop the first pawn, and the second (h6) still has nobody in front of it.
A queen appears with check — and there's STILL a free h6 pawn, pushed by a king who never had to pick a side.

Kubbel, 1927: five pawns, two kings, and a single question — capture on b6, or pass it by? The capture, a lifetime's reflex, only draws; the king moves lose; a5-a6!! alone wins, because a queen born on a8 will see diagonals her twin born on b8 never gets. A study about where queens are born.
Passing by
The two-queen race
The natural capture
The king who “improves”
Not the capture (axb6? only draws — see the trap), not a king move (all six lose: the e-pawn runs). The pawn WALKS PAST b6: black pawns only capture downhill, so a6 is untouchable — passed for good.
A lifetime's reflex: capture, and the passed pawn is right there. Yet count the race that follows —
Attacking e4, “keeping every option open”? The study is a matter of tempi, and this one LOSES:
The best defence: racing to meet the future queen, hoping to dodge her first check.
The other main defence: a queen each, may the better one win.
On a2 the black king hopes to hide… on the a-file, of all places.
No luck: the queen is born giving check.
The study's second point: the newborn queen scoops the e-pawn WITH check. The counter-promotion is dead before it ever existed.
A little housekeeping: …b4 is banned forever, b5 and b6 frozen — spectators until mate.
Setting the box: the black king is down to a1-b1.
The queen holds the box from afar; the rest belongs to the white king, strolling across the board (the pattern of the “Queen Mate” course).
Home.
Mate — while b5 and b6 watch, untouched. The black pawns never served at all: that was the verdict hiding behind move one.
Both queens are born on the same move. Draw? No — look at their cradles:
From a8 the long diagonal grants an IMMEDIATE check — the tempo that decides everything. (Born on b8 after axb6?, the queen has no such check: her lines run into the b-pawns — see the trap.)
The quiet move in the storm: the black king is caged (a4/b4), Qc3+ looms, and against it the e1-queen has not ONE resource — the tablebase grades every reply as lost.
Waiting — as hopeless as everything else.
The b2-pawn, silent since the study began, delivers the decisive check.
And the black queen dies at five moves old.
Queen against two frozen pawns: an elementary win. The race was rigged from 1.a6 onward — by geometry.

The same count as after 1.a6: queen for queen on the same move. But this one was born on b8 — and from b8, NO check: the b-file is plugged by Black's own pawns, the diagonal leads nowhere. Without that first tempo there is no geometry: a draw from end to end. All of Kubbel lives in the gap between a8 and b8.
The a5-pawn — the solution's hero — vanishes, and Black's queenside becomes an avalanche.

The white king is one square short everywhere: the a-pawn queens. The starting position, oracle-checked, in one line: ten legal moves — seven lose (all six king moves, and even b4), axb6 and b3+ merely draw, a6 alone wins. One correct move in ten: that is what a study is.

Four years before his world title, Emanuel Lasker composed this (1890): a white pawn ready to queen, a black pawn ready to queen, and a tempo-winning machine. White's king and rook walk down the board like a staircase — and at the bottom, the h-pawn falls together with the black rook.
The staircase
Grabbing h2 at once
Grabbing h2 one instant too soon
The ONLY winning move — even Rh6+ at once only draws. The king steps off c8: promotion becomes a real threat, and the black rook will have to chase two hares.
The black pawn was about to queen — removing it feels urgent. But look at the white king: he stands on c8, his OWN promotion square.
The only resource: drive the king away with checks.
And again c8=Q is threatened — the rook must run back.
Forced. Now watch the mechanism: while the black rook shuttles b2-c2, the WHITE rook gets to walk down one floor — with check, hence for free.
First floor down. The black king must move, and the whole exchange (check on b2, return to c2) restarts one notch lower.
This time the king has left c8 — so, ripe for the taking? No: the white rook is leaving the SEVENTH rank, where it held a second job.
Second floor. Count what Black's checks achieve: nothing — the white king always comes back; and every cycle, the white rook gains one rank.
The king goes back to work — note how he picks his square by the black rook's rank: never in line with a useful check.
The last floor that matters: this check shoves the black king ONTO the second rank — his own rook's rank.
Where to go? a4 and b4 belong to the white king. The king joins his rook… and becomes its problem.

Harvest time. The c2-rook is attacked and out of squares: staying means Rxc2+ followed by c8=Q+; trading means letting the pawn queen. The h-pawn White “neglected” for twelve moves falls at exactly the moment its fall wins.
Queen against rook: a known win — that is the “Queen vs Rook” course. The study itself is over: the staircase turned two facing pawns into a point of pure geometry.
And nothing left: without the white rook there are no descending checks, so no tempo machine. The black rook shuttles b2-c2 forever; the c-pawn will never queen. Draw.

There it is: h7 was guarding c7. The pawn falls, rook versus rook, draw. (Certainly not 5…Rxh2?? 6.c8=Q+ and the queen wins.) The staircase was no ornament: every check from Rh6+ to Rh3+ kept c7 defended AT A DISTANCE.

Your king sits in front of its 7th-rank pawn, the enemy rook harasses: this is the position ALL your winning rook endings are trying to reach. It is won by one famous manoeuvre — the bridge — four centuries old.
Building the bridge
The other king square
Without the bridge: the wheel spins
The relief trap
First drive the black king ONE file further: the bridge will need d7 and d8 free of tricks. Every move of the manoeuvre has its reason.

“Trade rooks, win the pawn ending” — NO: after Rxc2 the black king is inside the square and guarding the door. Not even a draw: a LOSS — king and pawn entombed on b7/b8, the black rook picks them off. Always check the ending AFTER the trade.
Ke8 amounts to the same — see the next chapter.
One square or the other on the same rank: nothing changes.
THE move of the course, baffling at first sight: the rook parks on the FOURTH rank, no higher, no lower. It is waiting for its king — this is the bridge's pillar.
Stepping out WITHOUT the bridge doesn't lose — but wins nothing: the checks never end, and the king's only shelter is… b8, where he came from.
Black can only wait: the rook must stay on the a-file — leaving it lets the king out for free.
The king FINALLY steps out — he never could without the preparation. The checks begin, and the plan expects them.
Towards the checking rook? No: towards b5, one step from the bridge.
A measured zigzag: the king isn't fleeing the checks, he is wearing them out.
The BRIDGE closes: the d4-rook interposes, the checks are over for good, the pawn queens next move. Four centuries this manoeuvre has been winning — it just won for you.
The bridge goes up identically.
Back to square one. Count: three moves played, zero progress. The bridge, proven by contradiction.
And the black rook resumes its post. Everything still to do — the right way this time.
Black says thank you. Kb8 and b7 will never move again; the black king escorts his rook to the feast.

Matisons, 1914: a white pawn two steps from promotion, a black rook that knows every road to stop it — from the front, from behind, by skewer. The white bishop blocks them ALL, one after another, selling itself twice along the way. A favourite study of everyone who likes pieces with several lives.
The bishop's two lives
The pawn in a hurry
Defending the attacked bishop
The king who flees the checks
The only win — and not for the check's sake: the bishop comes to PLUG the e-file. The direct 1.e7? runs into …Re1+! and …Rxe7 (see the trap); from now on that check no longer exists.
One tempo too soon: the e-file is still open.
Now yes. The rook can no longer stop the pawn from behind… on that file, at least.
A double idea: grab a pawn, and above all attack the e3-bishop along the third rank — if it moves thoughtlessly, …Ra8-e8 or …Re3 regains control of the pawn.

The bishop's first sale, and what a counter: it puts itself EN PRISE to the king to cut the a-file! The a3-a8-e8 road is closed; and taking costs the decisive tempo: 3…Kxa7 4.e8=Q and the rook is too late.
The e3-bishop hangs: defending it with the king — what could be sounder? But the study is not decided on THAT rank:
The rook switches floors: from below it threatens …Re1+ — the bishop left e3, the file is open again.
The only win, once more — here even all four promotions merely draw (e8=Q? Rf1+! and the e1-e8 skewer scoops the queen). The king walks TOWARD the announced check.
…Re1+ looms: stepping away from the rook looks prudent. It is the exact opposite of the solution — and the win evaporates:
The check comes anyway…
…and the bishop sells itself a second time, crosswise! The rook must take: otherwise the bishop keeps e1 covered and the pawn queens in peace.
Here is the bishop's real price: this tempo. The king attacks the rook…
…and again. Harried twice, the rook will never find time to return to the e-file.
Coronation. Queen against rook is a known win — see the “Queen vs Rook” course. The bishop died twice for this diagram: on a7 to cut a file, on f2 to buy two tempi.
The zwischenschach does all the work:
The rook gives itself for the pawn — the RIGHT trade:
…because what remains is a dark-squared bishop and the a-pawn — whose promotion square a8 is LIGHT. The wrong bishop! The black king camps on a8-a7: a book draw (see “The Wrong Bishop”).
…the rook slips BEHIND: a8 then e8, and the pawn is picked off on its own coronation square. Draw. Only 3.Ba7!!, plugging that road at the bishop's expense, won.
Now Black CAN afford the bishop: White no longer knows how to charge for the tempo it costs.
And the dreamt-of promotion even loses the game:
The e1-e8 skewer — the very one 4.Kf4! defused by walking toward it:
The queen is born and dies on the same square; rook against bare king, BLACK wins. The whole study in negative: without the bishop and the right king, every one of the rook's roads reopens.

King and pawn versus king: the endgame every other endgame eventually becomes. Exactly one square wins here — the one that takes the opposition. Understand it and you convert your endings; guess and you split the point.
The only winning square
The mirror: yielding the other way
The pawn that left too early
The king even eats the pawn
The hasty pawn, later on

The ONLY square that wins — everything else draws, including pushing the pawn. Kings face to face, one square apart, opponent to move: that is the OPPOSITION, and whoever doesn't hold it must give way.
THE universal mistake: pushing because pawns push. The win just evaporated — Black regains the opposition and will keep it all the way to stalemate.
Black yields one side (Kf6 mirrors exactly). The white king walks through the door just opened.
Yielding on the kingside changes nothing: the outflank then goes through d5, a perfect mirror of Kf5.
The OUTFLANKING: advance diagonally on the abandoned side, gaining ground with every step. The pawn can wait — king first, always.
Only now: the pawn advances WITH check, so without losing the opposition. Compare the “hasty pawn” chapter, where the same push one tempo too early draws.
The opposition regained, one rank higher. The mechanism repeats: opposition, outflank, pawn.
Even mid-winning-manoeuvre, ONE hasty push is enough: this move drives the black king to e7… from where he regains the opposition.
The pawn follows its king — never the other way round.
Opposition again, decisive this time: the black king has no space left behind him.
The king seizes e8: the promotion corridor is bought and paid for. The rest is an escort.
The pawn queens WITH check. Mating with the queen is another course — this one taught you how to get here.
Opposition regained. From here, replay the main chapter in a mirror.
The only defence, and it suffices: the black king stands ready to take the opposition the moment the white king steps up.
Pushing again threatens nothing: the black king plants himself IN FRONT of the pawn.
Trying to go round the wing is no better.
The blockade. The white king arrives, takes the opposition… and finds it useless: the pawn on e5 has stolen the very square the outflank would have needed.
The black king attacks the abandoned pawn: White will defend it forever — when he doesn't simply lose it.
The only defence — and it holds. In front of the pawn, at opposition distance.
Glued to the pawn: the white king can no longer advance to shepherd it, nor outflank. Textbook draw.

A passed pawn isolated on the far side isn't there to promote: it is a DECOY, and it gets sacrificed. Black's king must go and fetch it alone; during those four tempi, White's king crosses the board and eats the whole kingside.
The pawn gives itself up, the king crosses over
The pawn sets off alone, on the opposite side from everything else. It will not queen — Black's king has just enough time — and that is not its job: its job is to ATTRACT.
Black's king sets off. He has no choice: letting the pawn run loses on the spot.
Two squares travelled, and Black's king is already five files from his own pawns.
The pawn goes as far as it can. It is lost, and that is the plan: every square it gains is a tempo Black's king will have to spend coming back.
The blockade. The pawn will not get through — but Black's king is now nailed to the corner.
THE moment. White's king does not wait for the pawn to fall: he leaves NOW, while the other king is busy. Note he cannot go via f6 — the g7 pawn covers it — but f7 is open.
